claim_verdicts.evidence: EF Core docs, Adding Data: "Use the DbSet<TEntity>.Add method to add new instances of your entity classes. The data will be inserted into the database when you call SaveChanges". Extended this round (minor #4) with Updating Data: "EF automatically detects changes ... Simply modify the values assigned to properties and then call SaveChanges" — INSERT for Added, UPDATE for Modified.

EF Core docs, Using Transactions > Default transaction behavior: "By default, if the database provider supports transactions, all changes in a single call to SaveChanges are applied in a transaction. If any of the changes fail, then the transaction is rolled back and none of the changes are applied to the database." saving/basic.md NOTE: "For most database providers, SaveChanges is transactional. This means all the operations either succeed or fail and the operations are never be left partially applied." Npgsql is relational, so the provider condition holds here.

EF Core docs, Generated Values > Primary keys: "By convention, non-composite primary keys of type short, int, long, or Guid are set up to have values generated for inserted entities if a value isn't provided by the application. Your database provider typically takes care of the necessary configuration". Repo at stage-1: InitialCreate declares orders.id with .Annotation("Npgsql:ValueGenerationStrategy", NpgsqlValueGenerationStrategy.IdentityByDefaultColumn); db/schema.sql has `id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`.

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs` lines 8-23 are character-identical to the lesson block: the method builds `new Order { CustomerId, PlacedAt, Status, Items }`, then `await repository.AddAsync(order); await repository.SaveChangesAsync(); notifier.Send(order.Id, "order placed"); return order;`. Entities.cs declares `public int Id { get; set; }` on Order with no initialiser; nothing assigns it before those calls (the object initializer sets only the four other members).

`tools/extract-code DonHang.Infrastructure/EfOrderRepository.cs --tag stage-1 --lines 16-18` returns exactly `public async Task AddAsync(Order order) => await db.Orders.AddAsync(order);` and `public Task SaveChangesAsync() => db.SaveChangesAsync();`, identical to the lesson block. `db` is the primary-constructor parameter `DonHangDbContext db` on line 7, so the prose "db here is the DonHangDbContext itself" is exact.

Live run against the running stage-1 lab, 2026-09-24: POST /api/v1/auth/login (anh.tran@example.com) then POST /api/v1/orders with {"items":[{"productId":2,"quantity":1,"unitPriceVnd":450000}]} returned `HTTP/1.1 201 Created`, `Location: http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders/16`, body `{"id":16,"customerId":1,"status":"new",...}`; the request body supplied no id. donhang-api log for the same request: `notification for order 16: order placed`, i.e. notifier.Send read a real id after the save.
claim_verdicts.source: live run, localhost:8080 (donhang-api container); docker logs donhang-api

claim_verdicts.evidence: EF Core docs, change-tracking/miscellaneous.md "Add versus AddAsync": "Add ... do not normally access the database, since these methods inherently just start tracking entities. However, some forms of value generation _may_ access the database in order to generate a key value. The only value generator that does this and ships with EF Core is HiLoValueGenerator. Using this generator is uncommon; it is never configured by default." orders.id is an identity column (claim 3), not HiLo, so no database access at AddAsync.

EF Core docs, change-tracking/miscellaneous.md > Temporary values: "Temporary values are stored in the change tracker and not set onto entity instances directly", with the documented output `Blog.Id set on entity is 0` / `Blog.Id tracked by EF is -2147482643`. explicit-tracking.md: "temporary key values have been generated for each entity. These values are used by EF Core until SaveChanges is called, at which point real key values are read back from the database."
